div.p: Cache memories have been historically avoided in real-time systems because of their unpredictable behavior. In addition to the research focused at obtaining the worstcase execution time of cached programs (typically assuming no preemption}, some techniques have been presented to deal with the cache interference due to preemptions (extrinsic or inter-task cache interference). These techniques either account for the extrinsic (cache} interference in the schedulability analysis, or annuls it by partitioning the cache. This paper describes a new technique, hybrid partitioning, which is a mixture of the former two. It either provides a task with a private partition or accounts for the extrinsic interference that may arise. The hybrid technique outperforms the original two for any workload or hardware configuration. In conclusion, it represents a powe@l yet general framework for dealing with extrinsic cache interference.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Cache memories are becoming inevitable as a mean to provide the memory bandwidth requested by contemporary processors. For example, for the DEC Alpha 21064 running at 200 Mhz, one cache m i s s penalty is equivalent to the execution of 100 cached instructions [19].

However, cache memories have been historically disregarded in real-time areas because of their unpredictable behavior. The unpredictability of cache memories stems from two causes. Firstly, it is difficult to model the intrinsic (intra-task) cache behavior, because it is automatic, dynamic, adaptive, history sensitive and program dependent. Secondly, the multitasking nature of many real-time
kernels has caused the extrinsic cache interference among tasks to exist.

To address the first problem, some tools have been developed to calculate the worst-case execution time (WCET) of tasks taking into account the cache speed-up [5, 12,141. These tools assume continuity for the code execution, because from the point of view of program analysis, the number of preemptions is unknown. This limitation restricts the application of such tools to non preemptive scheduling policies like cyclic executives or co-operative scheduling.

However, this limitation is an inconvenience, since preemptive schedulers (in particular fixed-priority) are very flexible [15], and their theory has been extensively extended to meet practical requirements [2].

Two solutions can be used to make caches suitable for preemptive real-time systems, either using partitioning, or modelling the extrinsic (inter-task) cache behavior to incorporate the cache-related preemption delays in the schedulability analysis.
Partitioning techniques assign private portions of cache memory (partitions) to certain tasks, in order to guarantee that their code will remain in the cache while the processor executes other tasks.

Regarding the latter approach, in a previous paper [3] we presented CRTA (Cached Response Time schedulability Analysis) which includes a model of the extrinsic cache interference in RTA. RTA is an exact and efficient schedulability analysis for preemptive fixed-priority schedulers.

In this paper we propose a new technique, that mixes the former two. This leads to a method that can be adapted to the system (varying the number of partitions and their assignment to tasks), obtaining always the best results. In this technique (contrary to partitioning) all tasks benefit from the speed-up of the cache. On the other hand, com-p ed to CRTA, it reduces the extrinsic cache interference th t is accounted in the analysis.

div.head: 1Previous work
div.p: the following subsections, we summarise the sc emes in which the hybrid partitioning is grounded: CYTA and partitioning. 9 2.4 CRTA kRTA [3] is a technique that models the extrinsic cache intdrference in the conventional Response Time schedulabilify Analysis (RTA). RTA calculates the response time for itasks in the worst-case scenario (which corresponds to the critical instant in which all tasks are released at the same time instant). Comparing trivially the worst-case response time to the allowed deadline for each task, provides an exact and efficient off-line analysis for fixed priority preemptive scheduling.

The estimation of the extrinsic cache interference is divided into the assessment of the worst-case number of preemptions that may take place in the response time of a given task, and the worst-case cache-related delay that a preemption may inflict.

The worst-case number of preemptions is equated to the number of releases of higher priority tasks in the response time window for the task under analysis. The preempting model cannot discern if the preemptions are either suffered by the task under analysis (direct interference) or another higher priority task (indirect interference). The model only provides the total number of preemptions. Thus, the refill penalty (cache-related preemption delay) can only be characterised based on the preempting task. We can either consider a refill of the cache lines touched (in the worst-case) by the preempting task or consider a refill of the entire cache, depending on the available level of detail of the workload model. Conversely to this approach, Min et al proposed in [ 111 a technique to obtain a tighter bound of the extrinsic cache interference by the characterization of the preempted tasks.

The blocking time Bi refers to the maximum time that a task may yield execution to a lower priority task due to resource contention. For this kind of static analysis, the resources are typically handled according to a synchronization policy like the Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [20], and the term Bi is calculated based on it. Using this policy, the task under consideration may yield the CPU to a lower priority task once the former reaches a resource held by the latter, thus allowing preemption (which produces extrinsic cache interference) from lower priority tasks to occur.

To avoid this source of interference, the synchronization must be enforced by a policy that precludes a task from being blocked during its execution (and the blocking time B, has to be calculated according to it). For example, the Ceiling Semaphore Protocol (CSP) [17] can be used instead of PCP. CSP ensures that if a task is blocked, it will occur at the beginning of its execution. This way, additional preemptions due to blocking are avoided.

The equation is evaluated recursively until the time window w," stops growing (i.e. w,"+' = w,") or the deadline is missed (i.e. w?' > D, ). Since the final response time R, (R, = w,"+' = w,") increases monotonically with decreasing priorities, an initial value that can be used for w,' is RI.], while C1 can be used for wl '. In practical issues, CRTA delivers very good results when it is used with on-chip caches. These caches are extremely fast on a hit, which produces a large difference between running a task with or without cache. On the other hand, their size is typically small, thus it will be easier (and not too costly) to consider that the entire cache is refilled on a context switch. This way, it is not necessary to study the cache lines touched by each task.

div.head: Cache partitioning
div.p: Cache partitioning is aimed at improving the cache predictability by annulling the extrinsic interference by providing each task with a private cache partition. Additionally, a common partition may be used for data sharing or non critical tasks.

The cache partitioning approach may be implemented by software [23] or hardware [9, 101. The hardware scheme requires the cache be off-chip and some additional external circuitry for cache control. It introduces added latency to the processor cycle [7]. The software solution requires compiler support. The application code is relocated to provide exclusive mappings on the cache for each task. This scheme also introduces delays, in this case due to insertion of branches to interconnect the relocated pieces of code [16]. In addition, the access pattern of data structures must be changed in order to achieve exclusive mappings into the data cache.

In [8, 181 an algorithm is presented to optimally allocate partitions to tasks for SMART (Strategic Memory Allocation for Real-Time). The figure of merit of the algorithm is to reduce the overall utilization while guaranteeing schedulability. The cache is divided into S segments, and they are arranged in legal-size partitions (power of 2 due to hardware implementation constraints) to be assigned to tasks. When 0 segments are allocated to a particular task, such a task is not allowed to use a private partition.

In general, when a private partition is assigned to a task, there are two major implications. First, the task will be protected against extrinsic interference. Second, this task will not interfere with tasks with shared partitions. SMART only takes advantage of the first implication, since the cache speed-up is not accounted for non-cached tasks or task confined in a shared partition. Our technique instead, takes also profit of the second implication, since the preemptions induced by tasks with a private partition will not be accounted when calculating the extrinsic interference for those tasks with a shared partition.

In contrast to SMART (and cache partitioning in general), all tasks are cached in hybrid partitioning. This is very important because the difference between cache and memory speeds is getting larger since on-chip caches need to match CPU-speeds. In [8] it was measured that a program can run five times faster when a cache is used. However, this fact does not seem to be reflected in the examples given in [ 181 for the execution time of non-cached tasks. In conclusion, we assume that partitioning will deliver better results if a private partition is assigned to every task, even though it may be small (depending on the cache size and the number of tasks).

div.head: Hybrid partitioning
div.p: In [4] we showed that the partitioning technique suffers from intrinsic interference due to the small size of partitions resulting from providing each task with a private one (especially when the cache is small and/or there are a large number of tasks). Otherwise, if any task has not a private partition, its very poor execution time will jeopardise the overall system utilization.

On the other hand, CRTA suffers from extrinsic interference when the cost associated with a preemption is large (heavy tasks or large cache) or the number of preemptions is high (large number of tasks and/or high frequency).
This scenario provides motivation for the development of a hybrid technique (named Hybrid Partitioning), which is capable of performing well independently of the system configuration.

The hybrid technique proposed in this paper, is derived from the partitioning approach but the number of partitions can be fewer than the number of tasks. This way, partitions will be larger than they are for (fully) partitioning, allowing better intrinsic performance (by better exploiting of the temporal locality).

On the other hand, some tasks will share a partition. However, in contrast to partitioning (when some tasks do not have private partitions), these tasks are cached, in the sense that their WCET is calculated taking into account the cache speed-up. Therefore, the extrinsic cache interference that may take place has to be accounted in the schedulability analysis.

div.head: Assigning partitions to tasks and finding the optimal number of partitions
div.p: The first problem to be addressed is to determine the best number of shared partitions. Assuming N tasks and S partitions, if only one partition is shared, then S-I tasks will benefit from a private partition. If two partitions are shared, then S-2 tasks are now the tasks with a private partition. The latter case distributes N-(S-2) tasks in two partitions. However it does not help, because a task will produce/suffer extrinsic cache interference as long as there is another task using the same partition. The tasks with lower priorities than both colliding tasks, will suffer indirectly the interference, irrespective of whether they are mapped to another partition (either private or shared). In conclusion, the best choice is to provide only one shared partition.

Regarding the assignment of partitions to tasks, there are two rules: 0 Private partitions should be assigned to high priority tasks in order to reduce the occurrence of indirect cache interference (as explained in subsection 3.1).

Higher frequency tasks produce a larger number of preemptions. Thus, these tasks should have a private partition. However, the trade-off between the priority and period poses a problem: the partition assignment is not trivial for those schedulers that are not Rate Monotonic (i.e. lower priorities are assigned to tasks with longer periods). Therefore, an exhaustive search can be performed to cope with both problems: finding the optimal number of partitions and the optimal partition assignment to tasks.

The temporal complexity of the problem is exponential on the number of tasks: we have to test for every permutation of 2 things taken N at a time with repetition, that is P*(2,N)=2N. It is explained as follows. A task may or may not have a private partition. Thus there are two choices (two things), and a choice has to be performed for each task (taken N at a time). Finally the choice can be repeated (more than one task may have a private partition).

Since the problem is exponential, it will be solved by testing schedulability for each leaf of the tree (binary in this case), which corresponds with every possible assignment of partitions to tasks. Notice that the assignment of partitions is accomplished in the design step, thus, its complexity is not really relevant.

It is also possible to use techniques like simulated annealing or genetic algorithms to reduce the exhaustive search space. For example, simulated annealing has been used to find appropriate task allocations in distributed hard real-time systems [21]. The cache partitioning problem could be solved in this context.

Finally, in many cases a sub-optimal solution can be easily found and may deliver good enough results. We believe that very simple design heuristics will suffice to apply the proposed technique to take advantage of the use of caches in real-time systems.

div.head: Rate Monotonic scheduling
div.p: For the particular case in which the task-set is scheduled by the Rate-Monotonic, the problem of assigning partitions to tasks is simpler. For such a scheduling policy, lower priorities are assigned to the tasks with longer periods. Thus there is no doubt of which tasks must be confined in a common partition, since the ones with lower priorities coincide with the ones with larger periods. Thus, given S partitions, S-1 are used to provide private partitions to S-1 tasks, while only one partition is assigned to the remainder N-(S-I) lower priority tasks.

The problem is then reduced to finding the optimal number of partitions. The following describe an analytical way to determine such a number. However, if the hardware and software of the system are currently available, it is also possible to determine the optimal number of partitions by brute force, since the size of the problem is limited. The system can be exercised for the available number of partitions, and the best configuration is chosen.

Depending on the workload and hardware factors of the system, a different number of partitions may be more appropriate. There is a trade-off between the intrinsic and extrinsic cache behavior to calculate the optimal number of partitions. On one hand, larger partitions (due to low number of partitions) produce benefits in terms of better intrinsic behavior. On the other hand, smaller partitions (due to high number of partitions) imply shorter refill penalties and less extrinsic interference since more tasks may hold a private partition.

Fortunately, it is not necessary to have an accurate model of the workload to compare intrinsic and extrinsic behavior for a given number of partitions. We can calculate the speed-down ratios with respect to ideal cache performance for both intrinsic and extrinsic behavior. By multiplying both ratios, we calculate the overall ratio for each number of partitions to be considered. The ratios range from 0.0 to 1.0, being 1.0 the faster. The optimal number of partitions will achieve higher score for the overall ratio. The following explains how to calculate the speed-down ratios.

The model is a single procesvel direct-mapped instruction cache. It is characterised by the following parameters: 80MIPS processor speed, 40nS memory read time, and 8 words cache line size. The cache is accessed at processor speeds, and its size is varied through the evaluations.

Regarding the extrinsic interference, we consider that every preemption inflicts a full cache refill (for CRTA) or partition refill (for Hybrid or partitioning). This cost is easily calculated from the cache/partition size and the available memory bandwidth.

Regarding the intrinsic interference, it is necessary to determine the portion of time of the WCET that is wasted in memory stalls due to intrinsic cache misses. The total computation time is divided into two components: ideal execution time Ci(;deal, assuming all memory accesses are cache hits, and the time the processor is stalled due to cache misses Ci(stall). The sum of both times is applied to the schedulability analysis, but once the test is passed, only the utilization which corresponds to Ci(ideal) is plotted in the graphs, and it is called schedulable utilization.

For the sake of simplicity, we have considered averagecase miss rates rather than worst-case miss rates. The available techniques to obtain the WCET of cached programs deliver miss rates which are very close to average ones. The required level of accuracy for the evaluation allows such an approximation. We rely on the formulae given in [6], which is based on extensive empirical observation, to obtain the miss rates from the cache size, cache line size, and associativity degree. Given the miss rate, it is easy to obtain the stall time based on the cache miss penalty (memory read time), and the number of memory ref-

div.head: erences (MIPS' parameter x task execution time).
div.p: The workload used in the evaluation is a set of periodic and independent tasks inspired on the benchmark Hartstone [22]. All task's deadlines are equated to task's periods. Thus, the Rate Monotonic priority assignment can be applied, it being optimal. The default task-set is fully harmonic. Under these assumptions, a 100% schedulable utilization can be reached under ideal conditions (zero overhead). This allows us to completely isolate the effect of the cache interference from the timeline constraints. Thus, the system is jeopardised by the cache interference exactly by the difference between the resulting maximum schedulable utilization and 100%.

Although this approach may seem simplistic, it is sufficient since some common characteristics of real-time tasksets can be reduced to periodic behavior (sporadic tasks, precedence constraints, multi-deadline tasks) and thus implicitly assumed in the model, or even ignored (release offsets) due to the abstraction level of the used schedulability analysis.

The evaluation process is as follows. Given an initial utilization, we equally assign execution time to each task. From the execution time, the number of memory references is estimated. From the number of references and the cache configuration, we estimate the intrinsic cache interference. This interference is added to the initial execution time. The resulting execution time is applied to the schedulability analysis to determine if the task-set is schedulable for the given utilization. The schedulability analysis includes the extrinsic cache interference. For CRTA, the extrinsic cache penalty is the time to refill the entire cache. For Hybrid or partitioning, it is the time to refill the partition. Apart from the extrinsic penalty, no context switch cost is considered. This process is repeated until the maximum schedulable utilization is reached. Finally, only useful utilization is depicted in the graphs (without extrinsic or intrinsic cache interferences). A binary search was used.

div.head: Comparing Hybrid to both CRTA and Partitioning
div.p: In this section we compare the effectiveness of the approach described in this paper to both CRTA and partitioning (abbreviated PART).

As can be seen in Figure 2 and Figure 3 , the performance of CRTA is highly conditioned by the number of tasks and system frequency. The partitioning technique is only slightly conditioned by the number of tasks. The Hybrid solution is always above the other two, even for the largest cache size. This means, that even for the more demanding workloads (high frequencies and large tasksets) it is not necessary to fully partitioning the cache, because Hybrid technique with an optimal number of partitions performs better.
The curves depicted in the X-Y plane are the projections for the points with equal value. The values are specified below the name of each technique.

Figure 2 shows that for a large number of tasks, CRTA obtains a good bound with the smallest cache. Inversely, partitioning is better suited with the largest cache. Hybrid solution performs properly independent of the cache size. This is important, since other application requirements may condition the processor selection. The processor may hold a cache of undesirable size for the other techniques. Moreover, because of the current level of integration, a mid size (i.e. 32 Kb) cache memory is more common in contemporary processors.

As can be seen in Figure 3, the better utilization is obtained for low frequencies and low number of tasks. The important fact from this figure is that even though Hybrid performs as constantly as partitioning, the former can outperform the latter by 2096, which is a considerable gain in schedulable utilization. Figure 3 presents evidence as well of the limitations of CRTA for adverse workload situations (high frequency and high number of tasks). This delivers the important conclusion that a small cache and CRTA are not appropriate for any system configurations. In this case, only the partitioning techniques can cope with the system's demands.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: This paper has presented a general yet powerful framework for dealing with the extrinsic cache behavior. It enables the use of cache memories in preemptive real-time systems, notably increasing the maximum achievable utilization. It has been shown that the schedulable utilization bound obtained is higher and more stable (quite independent of hardware and workload factors) than for previous methods.
